\section[planear]{planear — to plan}

\label{lesson:ES-C509-planear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for current, then the Spanish for acceptable.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: planear}
\textbf{planear} — \textquotedblleft{}to plan\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Planeamos un viaje a México.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We are planning a trip to Mexico.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{planear} is \emph{plan}, \textquotedblleft{}a plan\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-ear}. \emph{Plan} came from French \emph{plan}, a drawing on a flat surface, from Latin \emph{planus}, \textquotedblleft{}flat\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{planear}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{planear}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{planear}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for current, then the Spanish for acceptable, then say \emph{planear} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does planear mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To plan\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[desear]{desear — to wish, to want}

\label{lesson:ES-C509-desear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for acceptable, then the Spanish for to plan.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desear}
\textbf{desear} — \textquotedblleft{}to wish, to want\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Te deseo un feliz año.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I wish you a happy new year.}
\end{quote}

In a shop, \emph{¿qué desea?} — what would you like?

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{desear} is built on \emph{deseo}, \textquotedblleft{}a wish\textquotedblright{}, usually traced to spoken Latin \emph{*desidium}, built on \emph{desidia}, \textquotedblleft{}idleness\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desear}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desear}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{desear}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for acceptable, then the Spanish for to plan, then say \emph{desear} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does desear mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To wish, to want\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la meta]{la meta — the goal, the finish line}

\label{lesson:ES-C509-meta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to plan, then the Spanish for to wish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la meta}
\textbf{la meta} — \textquotedblleft{}the goal, the finish line\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi meta es hablar bien español.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My goal is to speak Spanish well.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{meta} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{meta}, \textquotedblleft{}the turning post of a racecourse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): the post the chariots raced round became a finish line, then any goal. A learned word: the \emph{-t-} between vowels stayed \emph{t}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la esperanza]{la esperanza — hope}

\label{lesson:ES-C509-esperanza}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to wish, then the Spanish for the goal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la esperanza}
\textbf{la esperanza} — \textquotedblleft{}hope\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Todavía hay esperanza.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is still hope.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{esperanza} is \emph{esperar}, \textquotedblleft{}to hope, to wait\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-anza}. \emph{Esperar} is Latin \emph{sperare}, \textquotedblleft{}to hope\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el acuerdo]{el acuerdo — the agreement}

\label{lesson:ES-C509-acuerdo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the goal, then the Spanish for hope.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el acuerdo}
\textbf{el acuerdo} — \textquotedblleft{}the agreement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Llegamos a un acuerdo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We reached an agreement.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar de acuerdo} — to agree.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{acuerdo} is the noun of \emph{acordar}, \textquotedblleft{}to agree\textquotedblright{}, from spoken Latin \emph{*accordare}, built on \emph{cor}, \emph{cordis}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{}: hearts brought together. The stressed \emph{o} opens into \emph{ue}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el acuerdo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el acuerdo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the goal, then the Spanish for hope, then say \emph{el acuerdo} again
\end{itemize}
